title: 16 Days: Why so few women in Bangladesh ever see justice
excerpt: Three in four women have faced partner violence. Fewer than one in ten take legal action, and tribunals convict in about 3% of cases.

image.alt: Women and Children Affairs Minister A Z M Zahid Hossain speaks at the 16 Days of Activism national dialogue in Dhaka on 25 November 2026, in front of an orange campaign backdrop
image.credit: Press Information Department, Government of Bangladesh, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain)

content:
Three in four women in Bangladesh have faced violence from a partner. Fewer than one in ten take legal action, and only a few of those cases end in a conviction. This year's 16 Days of Activism asks why.

The 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence began on 25 November, the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, and run until 10 December, Human Rights Day. The global theme set by UN Women for 2026 is "Ensure justice, protect survivors, end impunity". Orange is the campaign's colour, a symbol of a future free of violence.

In Bangladesh, the theme lands on a well-documented gap. Violence against women is common, it is rarely reported, and when it is, it rarely ends in justice. This explainer sets out what the numbers show, where the system breaks down, and what to watch over the next two weeks.

How common is violence against women?

The most complete picture comes from the 2024 Violence Against Women Survey by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics (BBS) and UNFPA, published in October 2025. It found that 76% of women had experienced at least one form of violence from a husband or partner in their lifetime: physical, sexual, emotional or economic violence, or controlling behaviour. In the 12 months before the survey, 49% had.

There is one sign of progress. Recent partner violence fell from 66% in the 2015 survey to 49% in 2024. But the survey also found new forms of harm: 8.3% of women had faced technology-facilitated violence, such as sexual blackmail and image-based abuse.

Why so few cases reach the courts

The same survey shows how much of this violence stays hidden. Two in three survivors (62%) never told anyone. Only 7.4% of women who faced partner violence took any legal action, and the authority they turned to most often was a community leader, not the police. Fewer than half of women (48.5%) know where to report violence, and only 12.3% know the government's violence against women helpline, 109.

Even when cases reach a tribunal, few end in a conviction. Research by the Supreme Court and BRAC, cited at a Manusher Jonno Foundation (MJF) dialogue on 24 November, looked at 4,040 cases settled in 46 tribunals in 32 districts between January and June 2025. The conviction rate was 3%. About 70% of the accused were acquitted, and cases took 1,370 days on average.

The logic is a chain of drop-outs. Most survivors never speak. Of those who do, most go to family or community leaders. Of the few who file a case, most see the accused walk free after nearly four years. Each step teaches the next survivor that reporting is not worth the risk.

What the latest figures show

Rights groups and the police published new figures as the campaign opened:

  • Dowry: Police recorded 887 cases of alleged murder over dowry in the past five years, Prothom Alo reported from Police Headquarters data. Many families are pressured to settle informally and go to court later.
  • Rape: Odhikar has recorded 21,627 rape victims since 2001. More than half, 11,715, were girls.
  • Killings at home: Ain o Salish Kendra (ASK) counted 172 women killed by their husbands or families between January and August 2026, 108 of them by husbands, based on reports in 10 national newspapers.

These counts come from police files or media reports, so they capture only cases that someone recorded. The real numbers are higher.

Where the system is weakest

Services are stretched. Physician and politician Tasnim Jara told the MJF dialogue that staff of the 109 helpline, the 999 emergency service and One-Stop Crisis Centres are not paid regularly and are short of people, so survivors often get information rather than help. Kamrun Nahar of Naripokkho said the Ministry of Women and Children Affairs has Tk 5,196 crore for 2026-27, of which only Tk 428 crore is for development work, and called for crisis centres in every district and upazila.

Funding cuts reach survivors. UN Women warns that cuts to aid are reducing services and weakening the women's rights organisations that support survivors. In Bangladesh, many GBV programmes, shelters and legal aid services run by NGOs depend on donor money that has fallen sharply since 2025.

The law has gaps. The Domestic Violence (Prevention and Protection) Act 2010 does not clearly cover former husbands, because its definition of family excludes past relationships, lawyers told The Daily Star. A proposed amendment was approved by the Chief Adviser's Office but was not issued as an ordinance before the election, so it remains a proposal. Odhikar is also calling for a victim and witness protection law and for Bangladesh to withdraw its reservations to Articles 2 and 16(1)(c) of the UN women's rights convention, CEDAW.

What was said at the launch

The national campaign opened on 25 November with a dialogue in Dhaka organised by the UN in Bangladesh, the Ministry of Women and Children Affairs and the Local Consultative Group on Women's Advancement and Gender Equality. Women and Children Affairs Minister Professor A Z M Zahid Hossain reaffirmed the government's commitment to stronger institutional responses to violence against women and children, The Daily Star reported. Acting UN Resident Coordinator Carol Flore-Smereczniak said: "Laws alone will not be enough," and called for accountability, reliable data and financing for survivor-centred justice. Australian High Commissioner Susan Ryle said technology-facilitated violence should be treated as a human rights issue, not only a cybersecurity one.

Why it matters

For NGOs, the 16 days are more than a calendar of events. Legal aid groups, shelters, helplines and community programmes are the parts of the system that help survivors move from silence to justice, and they are among the services most exposed to the aid cuts. The campaign's call to "end impunity" will be tested by whether the government funds crisis centres, fixes the gaps in the law and speeds up trials.

What to watch

  • Begum Rokeya Day, 9 December, and Human Rights Day, 10 December, when the campaign closes.
  • The domestic violence amendment: whether the new government brings it to parliament.
  • One-Stop Crisis Centres and the 109 helpline: any announcement on staffing, pay and expansion to districts and upazilas.
  • Donor funding for survivor services, as women's rights organisations report cuts.

Devlens will update its 16 Days coverage every day until 10 December. If you or someone you know is facing violence, call the national helpline 109 (free, 24 hours) or the emergency number 999.
